to ascend to the stage of a Bodhisattva, to transcend the realm of Māra, and to enter into *sarvajñatā* (omniscience); to know that all phenomena are fundamentally inconceivable and thereby achieve perfect awakening,
adorned with concentration and wisdom— this is called the person of middle-to-superior faculties at the fourth stage, "Pervasive Destruction of Phenomena."

This is the vehicle of the ten dharmas. Even if one has extensively refuted all delusions by means of the causal continuity and mutual dependence, if one has still not entered [the path], one should reflect that within all phenomena there exists the nature of peace and bliss; one must only remove the disease, not the phenomenon itself.

It is like using a golden probe to remove the film while preserving the pearl, or like the artisan of Ying who removed the flesh while preserving the nose—how could one ever proceed with such one-sidedness?

To destroy the obstructing is to break through the blockage; now one must skillfully recognize what is open and what is blocked. If there is a blockage, it must be destroyed; if there is openness, it must be protected.
Just as the Wheel-Treasure of a Holy King can both destroy and bring peace, by virtue of this recognition of the open and the blocked, the blocked becomes open.
Afflictions are themselves Bodhi; when Bodhi is thoroughly realized, afflictions no longer exist. Birth-and-death is itself Nirvana; Nirvana...

In the state of quiescent extinction where there is no further birth and death, one is able to fulfill the perfect and wondrous factors of the path (bodhipakṣa-dharma), reach the shore of both phenomena and principle, ascend to the stage of a Bodhisattva, transcend the realm of Māra, and enter into *sarvajñā* (all-encompassing wisdom).

Knowing that all dharmas are fundamentally inconceivable, one then attains perfect enlightenment, adorned with concentration and wisdom, universally shattering the three delusions. This is called the person of middle-of-the-middle faculties regarding the fifth consciousness.

The complete mastery of the ten dharmas constitutes the vehicle. Even if one recognizes what is permeable and what is obstructed, if one is still unable to transform obstruction into permeability, one should contemplate that the present single thought-moment possesses the inconceivable nature and characteristics of the three thousand [dharmas]. This is precisely the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the perfect mind, the *smṛtyupasthāna* of the single mind, and the *smṛtyupasthāna* of all minds.
Through right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*), one rouses oneself; by taking the *samādhi* of the fulfillment of wishes as an object, the five [supernormal powers] arise.

By causing the roots to grow so as to form the five powers, harmonizing the seven factors of enlightenment, and proceeding upon the eightfold noble path, one opens the three doors of perfect liberation and enters the secret treasury.
Thus, one reaches the further shore of both phenomena and principle, ascends to the stage of a Bodhisattva, transcends the realm of Māra, and enters into *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Knowing that all dharmas are fundamentally inconceivable, one then attains perfect enlightenment with certainty.
The adornment of wisdom universally destroys the three delusions and realizes that all dharmas possess the nature of peace and bliss;
this refers to those of middling and inferior faculties who, in the sixth stage of the Path of Adaptation (*anuloma-mārga*), are fully endowed with the ten dharmas of the vehicle.

Even if one has refined the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga*), if the power of contemplative wisdom is weak and hindrances arise predominantly, one will be unable to enter the [next] stage; there must be matters from beginningless time [obstructing this].

If hindrances have not yet been eliminated, one should carefully examine which hindrance is predominant and manifests repeatedly, and apply its specific antidote through both principle-contemplation (*li-guan*) and practical application (*shi-xing*).

With principle-contemplation as the primary method and practical application as the auxiliary, practicing them in union while disregarding even body and life, one vows to realize the goal without ever slackening.
Through these two types of treatment—principle and practice—one is able to sever the two kinds of illusions of beginningless time: those of principle and those of practice.

Because the hindrances are cleared away, one suddenly attains realization; when the characteristics of the stage [of enlightenment] become distinct, one eternally transcends the net of Māra and enters into *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge).
Knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally inconceivable, one immediately achieves perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), adorned with concentration and wisdom.

Universally destroying the three delusions, one realizes the nature of peace and bliss and becomes fully endowed with the perfect and wondrous factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*). This is called the seventh pair for those of inferior and superior faculties.

The "Aids to Penetration" (pratipakṣa-prayoga) consist of ten dharmas that bring the vehicle to fulfillment. However, during the stage of the Aids to Penetration, even those of dull faculties will certainly derive benefit;
yet, if one does not understand the stages and positions, one may give rise to overweening pride (adhimāna), conflating the ordinary with the noble, thereby incurring no small fault.
Therefore, one must deeply examine oneself: Is this the ultimate realization? Is it partial realization? Is it a semblance? Or is it...?

Is this merely a slight degree of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*)? Once you have understood these stages, do not give rise to arrogance; for there will surely be various strong and weak māras to disturb true cultivation.
You must apply patience (*kṣānti*), remaining unmoved and non-retrogressive, and exert yourself through the five grades to ascend to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Having ascended to the ten levels of faith, the six sense faculties become pure, and you will accord with the Dharma of the Path; yet, as it is easy to give rise to attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), you must abandon such attachment to the Dharma.

Entering through love and having entered the stage of true reality, one has already attained the Great Principle, the Great Vow, the Great Adornment, the Great Wisdom, the Great Severance, the Great Universal Knowledge, the Great Path, the Great Function, the Great Expedient Means, the Great Benefit, and the Great Non-abiding.
This is called the person of inferior capacity who, by fully cultivating these ten dharmas, accomplishes the Mahāyāna; this is the Mahāyāna that travels directly through the four quarters.
Upon reaching the place of practice, one exhausts the cultivation of oneself; having exhausted the cultivation of oneself, one continues without ceasing the cultivation of others.

Thus, these ten vehicles of wondrous contemplation involve the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation, and the entirety of cultivation manifesting nature; they are neither horizontal nor vertical, yet they penetrate thoroughly both horizontally and vertically.

Appendix: The Three Bodies of Compassion and the Conditions for the Arising of Compassion Based on Birth. There are six distinctions: 1. When ordinary beings cultivate compassion based on birth, they achieve the merit of a Brahmā King;

its essence consists of attachment (*tṛṣṇā*). 2. When non-Buddhists cultivate compassion based on birth, they take the fruit of the Brahma Heaven as their goal; its essence consists of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
In the Tripitaka Teaching, the two vehicles cultivate compassion based on birth (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) as an antidote to hatred, conceiving of others as parents and relatives;

this takes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its essence. Bodhisattvas also cultivate compassion based on birth to extensively practice salvation, likewise taking conventional truth as its essence.

However, in both cases, they do not give rise to attachments such as "self" or "person," and these are accomplished by relying on the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). Fourth, the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

The Compassion based on Sentient Beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) cultivated through the vehicle of the *śrāvaka* is fully realized by relying on the contemplation of the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

It takes as its object the six realms of ordinary beings and likewise takes conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its essence. Fifth, in the gradual approach of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-naya*), one first cultivates the Compassion based on Sentient Beings, which also takes conventional truth as its essence.

By not giving rise to false attachments to a self, persons, and so forth, it is likewise accomplished by relying on the two types of contemplation of emptiness—both the analytical (*vicaya-śūnyatā*) and the essential (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). (The Ten Faiths)

(Analyzing emptiness as the essence of the ten stages of abiding being empty): In the sixth, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), one cultivates the "compassion based on birth-conditions" (*shengyuan ci*) within a single mind, knowing that the ten dharma-realms are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Because one regards every sentient being within these ten realms—viewed through this emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—as having been one's own parents and so forth, one can discourse upon the six levels of realization (*liu ji*) by taking wondrous existence (*miaoyou*) as the gateway.

The compassion with phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*) has four distinctions: First, the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas of the Tripitaka Teaching realize the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Consequently, they contemplate all sentient beings as being merely the four great elements and the five aggregates; thus, they do not give rise to anger or affliction, but deliver others according to their capacity.

This takes the contemplation of the emptiness of persons as its essence (although Bodhisattvas have not yet realized emptiness, they are able to cultivate it). Second, the practitioners of the Three Vehicles of the Shared Teaching realize that persons are fundamentally empty and that dharmas are likewise so.

1. The Two Vehicles of Illusion (Huan): They deliver beings according to their capacities; the Bodhisattvas’ great vows are all-pervasive, and both take the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as their essence.
2. The Separate Teaching of Successive Practice (Bie jiao cidi xiu): Practicing the Dharma-conditioned compassion (*dharmapratyaya-maitrī*), they know emptiness yet do not dwell in emptiness;

awakening to the dharma of dependent origination, they extensively deliver the nine realms, taking the contemplation that enters the provisional from emptiness as their essence. 3. The Perfect Teaching (Yuan jiao): Practicing within a single mind.
By means of compassion, one knows that the dharmas of the ten realms produced through conditions are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

by relying on these dharmas of the ten realms as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, one knows they lack intrinsic nature, and thus, through the gate of wondrous non-action, one can discourse upon the six stages of realization.

There are two distinctions regarding objectless compassion (*apratisthita-maitrī*): First, the distinct teaching (*bhedanaya*) of the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) does not take as its object sentient beings who are mere designations within the ten realms, nor does it take as its object the phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the ten realms; rather, it takes as its object only the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) of the Middle Way.

Therefore, it is called "objectless. It takes both the [conventional] characteristics and the Middle Way as its essence (if one has ascended to the first stage, it is then identical to the perfect compassion). Second, the person of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*) at the beginning...

The mind immediately realizes that each and every one of the three thousand dharmas is, in its very essence, the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Apart from this Middle Way, there is no other dharma;

subject and object are suddenly severed, and the inconceivable [power] of uprooting [afflictions] is attained. Because the doctrine of the "six identities" (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*) is established, there is the meaning of the "unconditioned compassion" (*nirālamba-karuṇā*) of the stage of practice-in-action (*prayoga-mārga*), up to the unconditioned compassion of the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-mārga*). Since these three types of compassion are discussed as being only a single essence of compassion, all three compassions are...
The three sublime abidings (*brahmavihāra*) all discuss the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*); as with the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), there are these various distinctions.

Compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are likewise. However, they are distinguished by name: giving happiness is called "loving-kindness," extracting suffering is called "compassion," feeling mental satisfaction upon seeing others obtain happiness is called "sympathetic joy," and having a mind free from attachment that views enemies and kin as equal in a single mark is called "equanimity."
